claims.text: The initial material is cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility.
HfNbTaTiZr has a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10^-4–10^-2 s^-1.
Poor oxygen resistance limits the alloy's practical high-temperature use in air.
An anti-oxidation surface coating is a relevant intervention for high-temperature use of this alloy system in air.
Surface aluminization will form a thin, continuous, uniform, and adherent Al2O3 layer on cast HfNbTaTiZr.
The alumina layer will act as an oxygen-diffusion barrier.
The oxygen-diffusion barrier will prevent rapid oxidation of the HfNbTaTiZr substrate.
The aluminide treatment will preserve the substrate microstructure during high-temperature air exposure.
Preserving the substrate microstructure will preserve the alloy's useful mechanical properties.
After approximately 100 hours in air at 1000 °C, aluminized specimens will oxidize significantly less than untreated specimens.
Aluminized specimens will have lower oxidation mass gain than untreated specimens.
Aluminized specimens will develop thinner oxide scales than untreated specimens.
The oxide scale on aluminized specimens will be more adherent than that on untreated specimens.
After oxidation exposure, the aluminized alloy's room-temperature yield strength and ductility will remain comparable to those of untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr.
After oxidation exposure, the aluminized alloy's yield strength and ductility at 1000 °C and strain rates of 10^-4–10^-2 s^-1 will remain comparable to those of the untreated alloy.
The oxidation benefit depends on the aluminide coating having an optimal thickness and uniformity.
Thermal cycling or mechanical loading beyond the tested boundaries may reduce coating adherence and performance.
The coating's long-term durability under cyclic thermal and mechanical loading is not yet quantified.
Possible coating–substrate interfacial reactions beyond the initial testing period are not yet quantified.
